title: Default and Keyword Arguments: Make Function Calls Shorter and Clearer
excerpt: Give parameters default values, call functions with keyword arguments, and avoid the classic mutable-default bug.

headings.text: The Problem: Repeating the Same Value

html:
A function that takes five values is hard to call: which value goes where? And if four of those values are almost always the same, repeating them in every call is tiring. Python solves both problems with two features that work together.

A default argument gives a parameter a value to use when the caller does not supply one, and a keyword argument lets the caller name each value in the call. (A parameter is a name in the function's definition; an argument is the value you pass in when you call it.) Together they make calls shorter and far easier to read.

The Problem: Repeating the Same Value

Here is a function that builds a sentence about where someone lives. Nearly everyone in this data lives in the same country, yet every call has to say so:

def describe(name, city, country):
    return name + " lives in " + city + ", " + country

print(describe("Asha", "Pune", "India"))
print(describe("Ravi", "Delhi", "India"))
Asha lives in Pune, India
Ravi lives in Delhi, India

Default Values

Write = and a value after a parameter to make it optional. Do you have to repeat the country every time? Not any more: if the caller leaves it out, the default is used:

def describe(name, city, country="India"):
    return name + " lives in " + city + ", " + country

print(describe("Asha", "Pune"))
print(describe("Meena", "Paris", "France"))
Asha lives in Pune, India
Meena lives in Paris, France

The first call omits the country, so the default applies. The second supplies one, and the default is ignored. There is one rule: parameters with defaults must come after the ones without. Python checks this before it runs anything, and reports a SyntaxError, which means the code is written in a way Python's grammar does not allow, so it refuses to run it at all:

def broken(a=1, b):
    return a + b
SyntaxError: parameter without a default follows parameter with a default

Keyword Arguments

So far, values were matched to parameters by position (these are called positional arguments). You can instead name the parameter in the call. These are keyword arguments, and with them the order no longer matters:

print(describe(city="Pune", name="Asha"))
print(describe("Ravi", country="Nepal", city="Kathmandu"))
Asha lives in Pune, India
Ravi lives in Kathmandu, Nepal

Positional arguments can be mixed with keyword ones, but all the positional ones must come first. Python rejects it the other way round:

describe(name="Asha", "Pune")
SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument

Why bother naming arguments if the order already works? Readability. Compare send(msg, 3, True) with send(msg, retries=3, urgent=True). The second one explains itself.

You Already Use Them

Built-in functions use this pattern too. Have you been using keyword arguments without knowing it? Very likely: print() has keyword parameters called sep and end with defaults of a space and a new line:

print("a", "b", "c")
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")
print("Loading", end="...")
print("done")
a b c
a-b-c
Loading...done

The second line replaced the separator, and the third replaced the line ending, so the next print continued on the same line.

The Mutable Default Trap

There is one famous gotcha. Look at this function, where the default is an empty list:

def add_task(task, tasks=[]):
    tasks.append(task)
    return tasks

print(add_task("write"))
print(add_task("test"))
['write']
['write', 'test']

The second call should have started with a fresh empty list, so why does it remember "write"? Because Python creates the default value once, when the function is defined, not each time it is called. Every call that relies on the default shares that one list, because a list is mutable: it can be changed in place (the method append adds an item to its end). The standard fix is to use None, Python's value for "nothing here", as the default and build the list inside:

def add_task(task, tasks=None):
    if tasks is None:
        tasks = []
    tasks.append(task)
    return tasks

print(add_task("write"))
print(add_task("test"))
['write']
['test']

Now each call that relies on the default gets its own new list. As a rule of thumb, use simple unchanging values (numbers, text, None, True) as defaults, and create lists or dictionaries inside the function.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonDefaultKeywordArguments.ipynb.

Summary

  • def f(x, y=10) makes y optional; the default is used when the caller omits it.
  • Parameters with defaults must come after parameters without them.
  • Keyword arguments name the parameter in the call, so order does not matter and the call reads clearly.
  • In a call, positional arguments must come before keyword arguments.
  • Defaults are created once, so never use an empty list or dictionary as a default; use None and create it inside.
